title: The Beginning of Wisdom
subtitle: Proverbs 1:1–33
description: The book names its purpose, a father warns his son off the gang’s road, and Wisdom calls in the street.
paragraphs: The book opens by naming itself and saying what it is for. “These are the proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel,” written “for gaining wisdom and discipline, for comprehending words of insight,” and “for receiving instruction in wise living and in righteousness, justice, and equity.” It is a book for the young and the simple, and for the already wise too: “To impart prudence to the simple and knowledge and discretion to the young,” while the wise are told to listen and gain more. This is not a story of things that happened. It is a father's teaching and a collection of sayings, and its whole weight rests on one sentence: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline.”

The first voice is a father's, and his first move is to point at a gang forming in the street. “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother.” Then comes the invitation he fears, quoted so the son can hear how it sounds: “Come along, let us lie in wait for blood, let us ambush the innocent without cause.” “We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder.” “Throw in your lot with us; let us all share one purse.” The father's answer is plain: “my son, do not walk the road with them or set foot upon their path.” The men setting the ambush are ambushing themselves, because “they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives.” Greed eats its owner: “Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors.”

Then a second voice takes the street, and it belongs to Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman calling where everyone can hear her: “Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square.” She is not hiding in a school or a sanctuary. She cries out at the city gates to the people passing by, and her question is aimed at the ones who keep walking: “How long, O simple ones, will you love your simple ways?” She holds out a real offer to anyone who turns: “If you had repented at my rebuke, then surely I would have poured out my spirit on you.” Wisdom in this book is never locked away from ordinary people. She is in public, calling, and the tragedy she names is refusal.

Her warning is as direct as her offer. “Because you refused my call, and no one took my outstretched hand,” there comes a day when the refusing runs out: “in turn I will mock your calamity; I will sneer when terror strikes you.” “Then they will call on me, but I will not answer; they will earnestly seek me, but will not find me.” The text gives her reason without decoration: “For they hated knowledge and chose not to fear the LORD.” What follows is not so much a punishment dropped from outside as a harvest: “So they will eat the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices.” A person who will not be taught ends up living on what his own way produces.

The chapter ends with the door still open to the one who listens. Wisdom's last word in her first speech is safety, offered to whoever turns toward her voice: “But whoever listens to me will dwell in safety, secure from the fear of evil.” The whole book will now unpack those two roads. One begins in the fear of the LORD and is taught, step by step, by a father who keeps saying my son. The other is the road of the gang, the scoffer, and the fool who despises discipline, and it ends eating its own fruit. Chapter 1 lays the foundation and lets the reader feel the weight of the choice before a single saying is given.

title: Seek Her Like Silver
subtitle: Proverbs 2:1–3:35
description: Wisdom must be dug for like silver, and the man who finds her learns trust, correction, and generosity.
paragraphs: The father now sets the terms of the search. Wisdom is not drifting toward his son; the son must go after her: “My son, if you accept my words and hide my commandments within you,” if you incline your ear, call out to insight, and lift your voice to understanding. Then the picture turns to mining and buried wealth: “if you seek it like silver and search it out like hidden treasure.” Only men who dig find silver, and the promise attached to the digging is not riches first but something underneath them: “then you will discern the fear of the LORD and discover the knowledge of God.” The reason is stated as simply as anything in the book: “For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.”

What wisdom does, once found, is guard. “He is a shield to those who walk with integrity,” and when she enters the heart she brings her own watchmen: “For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will delight your soul,” and discretion and understanding stand guard over the road. The dangers she guards against are two, and they will run through the whole book: the man who speaks perversity, who leaves the straight paths to walk in darkness, and the forbidden woman whose house sinks down to death. Against both, the end of the matter is land and life for one kind of person: “For the upright will inhabit the land, and the blameless will remain in it,” while the wicked are cut off and uprooted.

Chapter 3 holds the book's best known lines, and the father sets them inside a life of trust rather than technique. “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding;” “in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight.” Loving devotion and faithfulness are to be bound around the neck and written on the heart. Wealth comes under the same Lord: honor Him with the firstfruits, and the barns fill. Even correction is reframed as love rather than rejection: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke;” “for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights.”

Then wisdom is priced, and nothing in the market reaches her. “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, the man who acquires understanding,” because her profit beats silver and her gain beats fine gold: “She is more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares with her.” Long life is in one of her hands and riches and honor in the other, and the image the father finally reaches for is the oldest tree in Scripture's memory: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her.” This is the same God who founded the earth by wisdom, and the father's point is that the stuff the world is built from is being offered to his son as a way to live.

The teaching lands in ordinary duties before the chapter closes. A neighbor in need is not to be sent away with a promise when the means are already in hand: “Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act.” Envy of violent men is refused, crooked dealings are refused, and accusation without cause is refused. Over it all sits the contrast that governs the book: “He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble.” The wise inherit honor. The search that began with silver ends with a son who trusts, gives, refuses evil company, and receives correction as a father's love.

title: Guard Your Heart
subtitle: Proverbs 4:1–5:23
description: A father’s inherited teaching: guard the heart, for from it flow the springs of life.
paragraphs: The teaching now comes down a generation. The father tells his sons what his own father told him when he was “tender and the only child of my mother”: “Let your heart lay hold of my words; keep my commands and you will live.” The command at the center of that inheritance is a chase: “Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn from them.” Wisdom is to be prized the way a crown is prized: “Prize her, and she will exalt you; if you embrace her, she will honor you.” And instruction is to be gripped like something alive in the hand: “Hold on to instruction; do not let go. Guard it, for it is your life.”

Against that road stands the other one, described without romance. The wicked cannot sleep unless they do evil; they eat “the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.” The two ways are painted as light and dark: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday,” while “the way of the wicked is like the darkest gloom; they do not know what makes them stumble.” Then the father gives the command this whole section hangs on: “Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life.” Mouth, eyes, and feet all take their orders from that guarded spring: put away perverse speech, fix the gaze straight ahead, make a level path, and do not swerve right or left.

Chapter 5 turns the guard toward one named danger, and it does not soften the description. The forbidden woman's opening is sweet: her lips “drip honey” and her speech is “smoother than oil,” and “in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword.” “Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to Sheol.” The father counts the cost in advance: vigor handed to strangers, years given to one who is cruel, wealth feasting a foreigner's house. Then he lets the ruined man speak his own regret: “How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!” “I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly.”

The answer the chapter gives is not suspicion of desire but desire kept at home. “Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” The springs are not to scatter in the streets; they belong to the marriage: “May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth.” The picture is glad and physical and unembarrassed: “may you be captivated by her love forever.” Then the father asks the question the whole warning has been building toward: “Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?”

Underneath the warning stands an eye that misses nothing. “For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths.” The snare, in the end, is a man's own sin rather than the woman's strength: “The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him.” “He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly.” The guarded heart of chapter 4 and the guarded home of chapter 5 are the same lesson twice: what a man keeps, keeps him.

title: The Ant, the Fire, and the Snare
subtitle: Proverbs 6:1–7:27
description: The ant schools the slacker, seven things are named that the LORD hates, and a young man drifts into the snare.
paragraphs: Chapter 6 opens with small, practical traps. A man who has put up security for a neighbor's debt is told to treat his own signature like a snare on his leg: “Go, humble yourself, and press your plea with your neighbor.” “Allow no sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids.” “Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the snare of the fowler.” Then the father sends his son to school to an insect: “Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise.” The ant has no commander or overseer and still gathers at harvest, while the slacker keeps negotiating with his bed: “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,” “and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit.”

Next the father names what God himself hates, in the book's most famous counting line: “There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are detestable to Him.” The list walks down a body: “haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood,” “a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that run swiftly to evil,” “a false witness who gives false testimony, and one who stirs up discord among brothers.” Pride, lies, violence, scheming, perjury, and division are not private faults here. They are the things the LORD is said to detest, and the last of them is the man who splits brothers apart.

The rest of chapter 6 returns to the adulteress, now with the plainest logic in the book. A father's commandment is “a lamp,” his teaching “a light,” given “to keep you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress.” The argument is consequence, not squeamishness: “Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned?” “Can a man walk on hot coals without scorching his feet?” A starving thief at least pays sevenfold and is done; the adulterer faces a husband whose jealousy “will not be appeased by any ransom, or persuaded by lavish gifts.” “He who commits adultery lacks judgment; whoever does so destroys himself.”

Chapter 7 then shows the snare working, in the book's one extended scene. The father watches from his window: “I saw among the simple, I noticed among the youths, a young man lacking judgment,” crossing the street near her corner at twilight. The woman comes out loud and prepared, with sacrifice talk on her lips and a perfumed bed at home: “Come, let us take our fill of love till morning. Let us delight in loving caresses!” “For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey.” The young man never argues and never decides; he drifts: “He follows her on impulse, like an ox going to the slaughter, like a deer bounding into a trap,” “like a bird darting into a snare,” “not knowing it will cost him his life.”

The father's closing words come back to his sons with the sum of the whole section: “Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths.” “For she has brought many down to death; her slain are many in number.” “Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death.” The remedy he gave at the start of the chapter was attachment to wisdom herself, almost as family: “Say to wisdom, ‘You are my sister,’ and call understanding your kinsman.” The speeches are building toward a voice louder than the woman at the corner, and in the next chapter she speaks.

title: Wisdom Cries Aloud
subtitle: Proverbs 8:1–36
description: Wisdom stands at the crossroads and tells who she is: older than the hills, at God’s side in creation.
paragraphs: Wisdom takes her stand where the whole city passes: “On the heights overlooking the road, at the crossroads she takes her stand.” She cries out beside the gates, at the entrances, and her call is to everyone: “To you, O men, I call out, and my cry is to the sons of men.” What she offers first is not technique but character: “O simple ones, learn to be shrewd; O fools, gain understanding.” “Listen, for I speak of noble things, and the opening of my lips will reveal right.” “For my mouth will speak the truth, and wickedness is detestable to my lips.” In a book full of warnings about crooked speech, Wisdom's own mouth is the standard: “All the words of my mouth are righteous; none are crooked or perverse.”

She prices herself above the same treasures the father used, and goes further: “Receive my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than pure gold.” “For wisdom is more precious than rubies, and nothing you desire compares with her.” Then she introduces herself in the first person, and her household is named: “I, wisdom, dwell together with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion.” Her politics are stated in one line: “To fear the LORD is to hate evil; I hate arrogant pride, evil conduct, and perverse speech.” And her reach is total: “By me kings reign, and rulers enact just laws;” “By me princes rule, and all nobles who govern justly.” Whoever governs well, in this book's account, governs by her.

Then her speech goes back before the world. “The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old.” “From everlasting I was established, from the beginning, before the earth began.” She was brought forth when there were no watery depths and no springs, before the mountains were settled and before the hills, before a single field or speck of dust existed. She was present for every act of making: “I was there when He established the heavens, when He inscribed a circle on the face of the deep,” when He set the sea its boundary and marked out the foundations of the earth. Whatever debates readers have had over these lines, the text puts Wisdom beside God at creation, older than the hills, at home in the world He made.

Her memory of creation is not cold. “Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence.” “I was rejoicing in His whole world, delighting together in the sons of men.” Wisdom delights in people, and so her speech ends by coming home to them with an invitation to keep watch: “Blessed is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors, waiting at the posts of my doorway.” No one has to hunt her down. She is at the door every day, and the alternative to finding her is stated as starkly as anything she has said.

Her last word holds life and death in one sentence each: “For whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD.” “But he who fails to find me harms himself; all who hate me love death.” This is the voice the gang, the slacker, and the woman at the corner have been competing with all along, and she is louder than all of them because she was here first. The next chapter sets her table against one other table in the city, and every passerby has to choose which house to enter.

title: Two Houses
subtitle: Proverbs 9:1–18
description: Two houses, two invitations, one street: Wisdom’s feast against Folly’s stolen water.
paragraphs: The speeches end with two houses on the same street, both calling to the same passersby. Wisdom's house is built and finished: “Wisdom has built her house; she has carved out her seven pillars.” The meal is prepared before the invitation goes out: “She has prepared her meat and mixed her wine; she has also set her table.” Her maidservants carry the call from the heights of the city, and the guest list is the same one she has addressed all along: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” The menu is one sentence of bread and wine, and the promise under it is life itself: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed.” “Leave your folly behind, and you will live; walk in the way of understanding.”

Between the two invitations the chapter sets down how a person takes correction, because that turns out to be the hinge of everything: “He who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself; he who rebukes a wicked man taints himself.” “Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.” “Instruct a wise man, and he will be wiser still; teach a righteous man, and he will increase his learning.” Then the foundation line of chapter 1 returns, now as the center of the whole section of speeches: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.” Wisdom lengthens days, and the accounting is personal: “If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage; but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.”

Then the other house. “The woman named Folly is loud; she is naive and knows nothing.” She has built nothing, prepared nothing, and sent no one. She sits at her own door in the heights of the city and copies Wisdom's invitation word for word: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” Where Wisdom served her own bread and wine, Folly's whole menu is secrecy: “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” Stolen and secret are not the seasoning of her meal. They are the meal.

The chapter's last line is the coldest in the section, and it is told to the reader rather than to the guest: “But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.” The young man of chapter 7 is inside that house now, along with everyone who drifted toward a doorway because no one was watching. The speeches are over. A father has warned, Wisdom has called, and two women have issued the same invitation from two doors. What remains is the long collection of sayings, where every line will keep sorting the wise from the foolish in the ordinary business of mouths, hands, money, family, and kings.
That sorting starts under a new heading in the next chapter: “The proverbs of Solomon.” The sayings come one and two at a time now, each a small test of which house a reader is learning to live in.

title: The Proverbs of Solomon: Two Ways
subtitle: Proverbs 10:1–12:28
description: Solomon’s sayings begin: two ways weighed in couplets of mouths, hands, and honest scales.
paragraphs: A new heading opens the long collection: “The proverbs of Solomon.” The sayings come in pairs now, most of them built on a contrast, and the first one is domestic: “A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother.” The great sorting of the speeches becomes a line-by-line sorting of ordinary life. Money appears at once, and so does its limit: “Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing, but righteousness brings deliverance from death.” Work is weighed the same way: “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth,” and the harvest makes it a son's honor or shame: “He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful son.” Over the whole field stands a quiet confidence: “The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but He denies the craving of the wicked.”

The mouth gets more lines than any other subject in these chapters. “The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.” Love and hatred are finally speech habits: “Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions.” Knowledge is stored or spilled: “The wise store up knowledge, but the mouth of the fool invites destruction.” And volume itself is a warning: “When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise.” The best speech is priced like metal: “The tongue of the righteous is choice silver, but the heart of the wicked has little worth,” and the worst of it is slander and lying lips, while security belongs to the straight walker: “He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.”

Chapter 11 opens at the market stall: “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but an accurate weight is His delight.” Pride and humility get one line each and no wasted words: “When pride comes, disgrace follows, but with humility comes wisdom.” Riches are tested against a day they cannot survive: “Riches are worthless in the day of wrath, but righteousness brings deliverance from death.” Then the chapter turns generous. A city rises or falls on the mouths of its people: “By the blessing of the upright a city is built up, but by the mouth of the wicked it is torn down.” And money itself behaves strangely in open hands: “One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor.” “A generous soul will prosper, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed.” Even the family tree is wisdom's picture: “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise.”

Chapter 12 starts with the reader's own response to everything before it: “Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates correction is stupid.” The house stands or falls as a unit: “A wife of noble character is her husband’s crown, but she who causes shame is like decay in his bones,” and “The wicked are overthrown and perish, but the house of the righteous will stand.” Speech is work and wages: “By fruitful speech a man is filled with good things, and the work of his hands returns to him.” Anger exposes a man instantly, while “a prudent man overlooks an insult.” And rash words are drawn as a weapon against everyone near: “Speaking rashly is like a piercing sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.”

The chapter closes where the collection keeps landing: on truth that outlasts its opposite. “Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment.” “Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight.” Work and rest are weighed one more time: “The hand of the diligent will rule, but laziness ends in forced labor,” and the anxious heart is given its remedy in another person's mouth: “Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up.” The last contrast is the road itself: “There is life in the path of righteousness, but another path leads to death.” Three chapters in, the collection has already stated its whole method. Two ways, weighed in couplets, until the reader can tell them apart at a glance.

title: Speech and the Weighed Heart
subtitle: Proverbs 13:1–16:33
description: A gentle answer, a weighed heart, and the warning that pride goes before destruction.
paragraphs: The sayings continue, and the family is never far away: “A wise son heeds his father’s discipline, but a mocker does not listen to rebuke.” The mouth is still the main instrument: “He who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin.” Work keeps its old contrast: “The slacker craves yet has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied.” One of the book's saddest lines falls in this stretch, about waiting itself: “Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.” And company is destiny, stated as flatly as the book states anything: “He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed.” Discipline in the home is stated just as flatly: “He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently.”

Chapter 14 watches people closely. The heart has weather no one else sees: “The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy,” and “Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow.” Its most repeated warning in the whole book appears here for the first time: “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death.” The poor and their Maker are bound together: “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him.” Work is honest gain against empty talk: “There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty.” And the fear of the LORD stands as family shelter: “He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge.” A nation gets one line and it is enough: “Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people.”

Chapter 15 is the book's great chapter on the tongue used gently. It opens with the method: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” The soothing tongue is “a tree of life,” while a perverse one “crushes the spirit.” God's sight covers the argument: “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good.” Contentment is priced against wealth twice over: “Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil,” and “Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred.” Counsel multiplies success: “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.” Timing is half of wisdom: “A man takes joy in a fitting reply,” and “how good is a timely word!” The chapter ends by joining humility to the book's foundation: “The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, and humility comes before honor.”

Chapter 16 turns upward, to a God who weighs what men can only plan. “The plans of the heart belong to man, but the reply of the tongue is from the LORD.” “All a man’s ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are weighed out by the LORD.” “Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved.” Even the famous summary of the human condition here is double: “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.” Kings come under the same weighing: honest scales are the LORD's concern, and “a throne is established through righteousness.” Wisdom is priced above gold one more time, and then the book's most quoted warning lands: “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.”

The stretch closes with the tongue sweetened and the temper governed. “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.” The way that seems right appears a second time, word for word, as if the collection refuses to let it be forgotten. Self-control outranks conquest: “He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city.” And the last line of the chapter hands even chance back to God: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.” Men plan, speak, work, and cast lots. The weighing is not theirs.

title: Life and Death in the Power of the Tongue
subtitle: Proverbs 17:1–22:16
description: Life and death in the power of the tongue, kindness to the poor as a loan to the LORD, and a good name.
paragraphs: These chapters keep returning to the dinner table and the friendship that survives hard times: “Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife.” The LORD tests hearts the way fire tests metal: “A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts.” Rebuke is measured by the depth it cuts: “A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool.” Then friendship gets the book's most durable line: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.” The same stretch warns the tongue that starts fires: “To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out,” and it mocks the man who signs pledges carelessly, the theme the father raised back in chapter 6.

Chapter 18 opens with the loner: “He who isolates himself pursues selfish desires; he rebels against all sound judgment.” The fool's mouth is his own worst enemy: “A fool’s mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare to his soul.” Gossip goes down like food: “The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being.” Against all of it stands the chapter's tower: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe.” Wealth builds a wall only in the imagination by contrast, and humility keeps its place before honor. Courtroom wisdom appears too: “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him.” Then the tongue receives the sentence this episode is named for: “Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.”

Chapter 19 weighs poverty and integrity without flinching: “Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a fool whose lips are perverse.” Wealth gathers friends and poverty loses them, and the book says so without pretending otherwise. Generosity is given an astonishing ledger: “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.” The slacker appears at his most comic and most sad: “The slacker buries his hand in the dish; he will not even bring it back to his mouth.” Human planning bows again: “Many plans are in a man’s heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail,” and the fear of the LORD is rest itself: “The fear of the LORD leads to life, that one may rest content, without visitation from harm.”

Chapters 20 and 21 bring kings, wine, and work into the same light. “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise.” The slacker misses his season: “The slacker does not plow in season; at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there.” Honest trade is worship's neighbor: “Differing weights and unequal measures” are named together in one breath, and “both are detestable to the LORD.” The king's heart is not his own to steer: “The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases.” Justice outranks sacrifice: “To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice.” And preparation ends where it must: “A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD.”

The first collection draws toward its close with the sayings about name and children that readers have carried for centuries. “A good name is more desirable than great riches; favor is better than silver and gold.” Rich and poor meet on level ground exactly once: “The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all.” Humility is given its wages: “The rewards of humility and the fear of the LORD are wealth and honor and life.” Then the line every parent knows: “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” It stands as the text prints it, a saying of the book's wisdom rather than a signed contract. The stretch ends on the borrower and the skilled man: the borrower is slave to the lender, and “Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will be stationed in the presence of kings.” The next voice is not Solomon's. The book itself changes speakers.

title: The Thirty Sayings of the Wise
subtitle: Proverbs 22:17–24:34
description: The words of the wise: thirty sayings guarding the poor, the drunkard’s woe, and a sluggard’s ruined vineyard.
paragraphs: Midway through chapter 22 the speaker changes, and the book says so: “Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise,” and “apply your mind to my knowledge.” The sayings that follow are counted by their own author: “Have I not written for you thirty sayings about counsel and knowledge,” written “to show you true and reliable words, that you may soundly answer those who sent you?” Their stated aim is trust: “So that your trust may be in the LORD, I instruct you today,” “yes, you.” Where Solomon's collection sorted life in couplets, these thirty come as short teachings, several lines each, addressed to a reader who seems to serve at a court and answer to senders.

The first teachings guard the weak at the gate. “Do not rob a poor man because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the gate,” “for the LORD will take up their case and will plunder those who rob them.” Angry company is refused for what it teaches: “Do not make friends with an angry man, and do not associate with a hot-tempered man,” “or you may learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.” Pledges are refused again, ancient boundary stones are left where the fathers put them, and the fields of the fatherless are fenced by a person: “Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless,” “for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you.” A young reader is told what to buy and never sell: “Invest in truth and never sell it,” “in wisdom and instruction and understanding.”

The longest of the thirty is a portrait of the drunkard, drawn as a series of questions: “Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has contentions? Who has complaints? Who has needless wounds? Who has bloodshot eyes?” “Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks.” The wine is beautiful and the book admits it: “Do not gaze at wine while it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly.” “In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper.” The drunkard's own voice closes the portrait, half drowned and already thirsty: “They struck me, but I feel no pain! They beat me, but I did not know it! When can I wake up to search for another drink?” Around it stand quieter teachings: do not wear yourself out to get rich, do not envy sinners, listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.

Chapter 24 turns from appetite to courage. A house is built the way a life is: “By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established.” Strength is for rescuing, not for excuses: “Rescue those being led away to death, and restrain those stumbling toward the slaughter,” and the plea of ignorance is answered before it is made: “does not He who weighs hearts consider it?” Falling is not the end of a righteous man: “For though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up; but the wicked stumble in bad times.” Gloating over an enemy's fall is refused, envy of the wicked is refused, and revenge is refused in the first person. Do not say it: “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work.”

Then a short appendix speaks under its own heading: “These also are sayings of the wise.” Partiality in judgment heads it: “To show partiality in judgment is not good.” An honest answer is given a kiss's value: “An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips.” Work order is set for builders: “Complete your outdoor work and prepare your field; after that, you may build your house.” The section closes with the teacher walking past a ruin and learning from it in the first person: “I went past the field of a slacker and by the vineyard of a man lacking judgment.” “Thorns had grown up everywhere, thistles had covered the ground, and the stone wall was broken down.” “I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction,” and the lesson is the ant chapter's refrain returned: a little sleep, a little slumber, and poverty like a robber. The wise have spoken. The next collection carries a king's name in its heading again, but copied by other hands.

title: Copied by the Men of Hezekiah
subtitle: Proverbs 25:1–29:27
description: Sayings copied by Hezekiah’s men: the fool answered and not answered, iron sharpening iron, mercy for the confessed.
paragraphs: The last Solomon collection opens under a copyist's heading: “These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah.” Solomon had been dead for centuries when Hezekiah's scribes gathered these, and the book prints that fact without embarrassment. Kings fill the opening sayings: “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out,” and a throne is made safe the same way it was in chapter 16: “Remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.” Speech at court is pictured at its best: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver,” and a wise rebuke is jewelry to a listening ear. Even the enemy is fed: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink,” “you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.”

Chapter 26 is the book's gallery of the fool, and it holds the pair of sayings this whole series has promised not to explain away. They stand back to back: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him.” “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes.” The book sets them side by side and moves on, as if wisdom is knowing which one the moment in front of you calls for. Around them the fool is drawn in a dozen strokes: honor on him is snow in summer, a proverb in his mouth is a thorn in a drunkard's hand, and his folly is a habit he returns to: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly.” There is one figure in the chapter judged worse off than the fool: “Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.”

The slacker shares the chapter, still inventing lions. His excuse is quoted whole: “A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!” He turns on his bed like a door on its hinges, and he buries his hand in the dish a second time in the book, too tired to lift it back. Chapter 27 turns warmer. Friendship is tested by honesty: “Better an open rebuke than love that is concealed,” and “The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” Its most carried line is about what friends do to each other over years: “As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.” The heart is a mirror: “As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man.” And the farmer is told to know his flocks, because riches and crowns both run out.

Chapter 28 is the collection's justice chapter, and it opens at a run: “The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion.” Rulers are weighed by their treatment of the poor, and a land in rebellion multiplies princes while understanding keeps order. Concealment and confession get the book's clearest mercy line: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy.” The poor are not a theme to visit but a test to pass: “Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who hides his eyes will receive many curses,” and a rich man's self-image does not survive a discerning poor man: “A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him.”

Chapter 29 gathers rulers, children, and anger into the book's last long look at power. “When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.” A king's fairness to the poor is dynastic: “A king who judges the poor with fairness,” and “his throne will be established forever.” Discipline returns as rest for the parent who gives it: “Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.” The fool and the wise man are set by their anger one last time: “A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back.” Then the line generations have quoted about vision, and the snare that ends the collection's warnings: “Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint; but blessed is he who keeps the Law.” “The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.” Two voices remain in the book, and neither of them is Solomon.

title: Agur: I Am Weary, O God
subtitle: Proverbs 30:1–33
description: Agur confesses his ignorance, prays for neither poverty nor riches, and learns from ants and eagles.
paragraphs: A new name signs the chapter, a man the book never mentions anywhere else: “These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh.” His oracle opens not with authority but with exhaustion and a confession no other wisdom teacher in the book makes about himself: “I am weary, O God, and worn out.” “Surely I am the most ignorant of men, and I lack the understanding of a man.” “I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One.” Then the ignorant man asks the largest questions in the book: “Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands? Who has bound up the waters in His cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth?” The questions end with a name he does not supply: “What is His name, and what is the name of His Son,” “surely you know!”

Out of that humility comes the book's strongest sentence about God's words themselves: “Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.” And its warning about improving on them: “Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.” Agur's one prayer follows, and it asks for two things only. The first is distance from falsehood. The second is the most famous request in the chapter: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion.” He gives his reasons in both directions. Too much, and he might deny the God who fed him: “Otherwise, I may have too much and deny You,” and say the words he dreads: “Who is the LORD?” Too little, and he might steal and profane the name he loves. The middle is not mediocrity to Agur. It is protection for his honesty.

Then Agur teaches the way the whole chapter teaches, by counting and watching. Four generations are sketched by their sins: those who curse their parents, those pure in their own eyes and unwashed, the haughty, and those whose teeth are swords devouring the poor. The leech has two daughters named Give and Give, and behind them stand the things that never say enough: “Sheol, the barren womb, land never satisfied with water, and fire that never says, ‘Enough!’” Wonders follow, things too wonderful for the man who confessed his ignorance at the start: “There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand,” “the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a snake on a rock, the way of a ship at sea, and the way of a man with a maiden.” The earth trembles under its own list of upstarts, and a servant on a throne heads it.

His best loved list is the smallest one. “Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly wise.” “The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer.” The rock badgers make their homes in the rocks. “the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation.” And the lizard, catchable in a hand, is found in kings' palaces. The stately walkers close the animal teachings, a lion refusing retreat, a strutting rooster, a he-goat, and a king with his army around him. Smallness with wisdom beats greatness without it, which is the confession the chapter began with, now proved from the fields.

Agur ends by turning his own medicine on the reader. “If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth.” His last picture is a kitchen and a nose: “For as the churning of milk yields butter, and the twisting of the nose draws blood, so the stirring of anger brings forth strife.” The man who said he lacked the understanding of a man has left the book's most honest prayer and some of its sharpest eyes. One voice remains, and it belongs to a mother.

title: Lemuel, and the Wife of Noble Character
subtitle: Proverbs 31:1–31
description: A mother’s teaching for a king, and the book’s closing portrait of the wife of noble character.
paragraphs: The book's last signature belongs to a king taught by his mother: “These are the words of King Lemuel,” and what follows is “the burden that his mother taught him.” She addresses him the way the father addressed his son at the start, but from a throne's side: “What shall I say, O my son? What, O son of my womb? What, O son of my vows?” Her warnings are a queen mother's, aimed at what ruins kings: “Do not spend your strength on women or your vigor on those who ruin kings.” Wine is refused to rulers for the sake of the ruled: “It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine,” “lest they drink and forget what is decreed, depriving all the oppressed of justice.”

Her positive command is the one her son's throne exists for: “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed.” “Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy.” The speeches that opened this book with a father warning his son close with a mother commanding a king to speak for people who cannot speak for themselves. Then the book does something no earlier chapter prepared for. It ends not with a king at all, but with a portrait, verse by verse, of a woman: “A wife of noble character, who can find? She is far more precious than rubies.” The rubies of chapter 3 and chapter 8, wisdom's own price, are the price set on her.

The portrait is built out of work. “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value.” “She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life.” She selects wool and flax and works with eager hands. “She is like the merchant ships, bringing her food from afar.” “She rises while it is still night to provide food for her household and portions for her maidservants.” She appraises a field and buys it, and plants a vineyard from her earnings. “She girds herself with strength and shows that her arms are strong.” Her lamp stays lit into the night, her hands hold the distaff and the spindle, and her trade is real: she makes linen garments and sells them. Her husband, meanwhile, “is known at the city gates, where he sits among the elders of the land.” His standing and her work hold each other up.

Her strength is not spent only inside her own walls. “She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.” Snow does not frighten her household, because she has clothed them ahead of it. “Strength and honor are her clothing, and she can laugh at the days to come.” Her mouth matches the book's whole teaching on speech: “She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue.” She “does not eat the bread of idleness,” and the response of her house is praise spoken out loud: “Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband praises her as well,” “Many daughters have done noble things, but you surpass them all!”

The portrait, and the entire book, close on the foundation line of chapter 1, now worn by a person: “Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.” “Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates.” Wisdom began this book calling in the streets as a woman with a house and a table. It ends with a woman in an ordinary house whose work, speech, generosity, and fear of the LORD are wisdom with its sleeves rolled up. The father's first sentence and the mother's last portrait say the same thing from two ends of the book: the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins, and a life built on it is the proof.
